questions.q: What does a 'lock-free' guarantee actually promise?
options: That every thread finishes in a bounded number of steps regardless of other threads
That the code contains no std::mutex anywhere in the source file
That at least one thread is always able to make progress, even if other threads are suspended at the worst possible moment
That the program never uses std::atomic
questions.explain: Lock-free means the overall system always makes progress because no thread can be permanently blocked by another suspended or stalled thread — it is weaker than wait-free, which guarantees every thread (not just one) finishes in bounded steps.

questions.q: In the lock-free stack push example, what happens when compare_exchange_weak fails?
options: The program throws an exception and terminates
The new node is permanently lost and must be reallocated from scratch
new_node->next is refreshed with the current head, and the loop retries the swap
The thread acquires a mutex and retries under lock
questions.explain: compare_exchange_weak writes the atomic's actual current value into its expected-value argument on failure, so new_node->next is already updated for the next iteration of the retry loop.

questions.q: What is the ABA problem in lock-free programming?
options: A thread reads a pointer, that memory is freed and reallocated to a different object at the same address, and a later check wrongly concludes nothing changed
Two threads both trying to acquire the same mutex at the same time
A compiler warning about unused atomic variables
A stack overflow caused by too many recursive CAS retries
questions.explain: The ABA problem occurs when a pointer value appears unchanged across two reads, but the underlying object was actually freed and a new, different object was allocated at the same address in between.

options: Two threads sharing the same std::mutex incorrectly
Unrelated atomic variables used by different threads that happen to occupy the same CPU cache line, causing contention-like slowdowns with no actual logical race
Passing a shared_ptr by value instead of by reference
Two threads calling the same function with different arguments
questions.explain: False sharing happens when independent variables land on the same cache line; a write by one core invalidates the cache line for other cores, producing performance costs that resemble contention even without any shared logical state.

questions.q: What is the recommended default approach to using lock-free data structures in production code?
options: Always hand-roll a custom lock-free structure for every shared-state problem
Avoid lock-free techniques entirely in all cases
Prefer a reviewed, widely used lock-free library, and reserve hand-rolled lock-free code for cases where a mutex has been measured to be the actual bottleneck
Use lock-free code only for single-threaded programs
questions.explain: Hand-rolled lock-free code is prone to subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs like the ABA problem. The practical default is to use a trusted, tested library and only write custom lock-free code when profiling has shown a mutex is genuinely the bottleneck.
